title: Assisted Quantum Teleportation
authors: Kaavya Iyer Mithilesh Kumar
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18896v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Teleportation through a non-maximally entangled pair, e.g., [MATH], induces a noisy channel and cannot achieve deterministic unit-fidelity transmission unless [MATH]. We introduce a framework of in which a third party (the ``Bank'') supplies auxiliary multipartite entanglement to restore a perfect Bell pair on the original [MATH] registers. We analyze two operational roles for the Bank: a Bank-measures model (measurement and broadcast) and a transfer model (the Bank transfers its subsystem and then leaves). For GHZ-class and W-class assistance we derive explicit feasibility regions for deterministic restoration and show an operational inequivalence for W resources. We further characterize finite-shot optimal success probabilities for probabilistic restoration and formulate Bank-measures feasibility for general pure Bank resources as a minimax optimization.
tldr: This paper introduces a framework where a third party (Bank) supplies auxiliary multipartite entanglement to restore perfect teleportation over non-maximally entangled pairs, analyzing GHZ and W states for deterministic and probabilistic restoration.
motivation: Standard teleportation using non-maximally entangled pairs results in a noisy channel and cannot achieve deterministic unit-fidelity transmission. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by leveraging additional entanglement from a third party.
method: The authors propose two operational models for the Bank: Bank-measures (measurement and broadcast) and transfer model (Bank transfers its subsystem and leaves). They derive feasibility regions for deterministic restoration using GHZ-class and W-class assistance, and characterize finite-shot optimal success probabilities for probabilistic restoration via minimax optimization.
result: Explicit feasibility regions for deterministic restoration are derived for GHZ and W states, showing operational inequivalence for W resources. For probabilistic restoration, finite-shot optimal success probabilities are characterized, and Bank-measures feasibility for general pure Bank resources is formulated as a minimax optimization.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to restore perfect teleportation using auxiliary entanglement, with implications for quantum communication protocols and network configurations. Future work may explore other resource states and experimental implementations.

title: Quantum Viterbi Algorithm
authors: Luigi Accardi, Abdessatar Souissi, El Gheteb Soueidi, Farrukh Mukhamedov, Mohamed Rhaima
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a quantum Viterbi decoding algorithm for hidden quantum Markov models (HQMMs) motivated by quantum information processing and quantum algorithms. Given a finite sequence of measurement outcomes, the algorithm identifies hidden quantum trajectories that maximize a joint decoding functional, serving as a genuine quantum analogue of the classical Viterbi score. Unlike classical hidden Markov models, where decoding optimizes over a finite discrete state space, our method performs optimization over a continuous manifold of pure quantum effects, thereby exploiting coherent superpositions in the hidden memory. We prove a strict quantum advantage: coherent hidden trajectories can achieve decoding scores that strictly exceed any classical strategy constrained to diagonal (commuting) effects, even when both models share the same observed statistics. These results position quantum Viterbi decoding as a concrete quantum algorithmic primitive for sequential decision-making, with direct applications to quantum memories, quantum communication with memory, and near-term quantum machine learning on NISQ devices.
tldr: The paper introduces a quantum Viterbi algorithm for hidden quantum Markov models that achieves a strict advantage over classical decoding by exploiting coherent superpositions.
motivation: To develop a quantum analogue of the classical Viterbi algorithm for sequential decision-making in quantum systems, with potential applications in quantum communication and memory.
method: The authors formulate a decoding optimization over a continuous manifold of pure quantum effects, contrasting with classical discrete state space optimization, and prove a strict quantum advantage.
result: Coherent hidden trajectories can achieve decoding scores strictly exceeding any classical strategy constrained to diagonal effects, even when observed statistics are identical.
conclusion: The quantum Viterbi algorithm provides a concrete primitive for quantum machine learning and quantum communication with memory, with implications for NISQ devices.

title: Non-Stationary Decoherence In Superconducting Qubits: Memory Multi-Fractional Brownian Motion And A Time-Dependent Quantum Brownian Motion Extension
authors: Mahboob Ul Haq
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18914v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building upon our prior work [1], we present a unified stochastic drift model (SdM) for superconducting charge qubits based on memory multi-fractional Brownian motion (mmFBM). The classical sector employs a time-dependent Hurst exponent H(t) and adaptive memory kernel K(t,s), capturing non-stationary 1/f^beta noise and long-range temporal correlations inaccessible to conventional models. The quantum extension is formulated via a time-dependent Caldeira--Leggett environment with spectral density J(omega;t) = eta(t) omega_c^{1-s(t)} omega^{s(t)} exp(-omega/omega_c), where s(t) = 2H(t)-1, consistently reproducing beta(t) = 2H(t)-1. Four central results emerge: (1) relaxation and noise amplitudes act independently on energy decay; (2) time-varying H(t) matches experimental 1/f spectra more accurately than any constant exponent; (3) adaptive kernel dynamics preserve correlations without artificial damping; and (4) simulations predict coherence times (T1 ~ 5.00 x 10^6 ns, T2 ~ 4.18 x 10^5 ns) consistent with theory when charge noise dominates. The qubit exhibits stretched-exponential Ramsey and echo decay, non-Markovian dephasing, and a temperature-driven quantum-to-classical crossover. We derive the effective time-local Lindblad master equation, establish the classical mmFBM limit at high temperatures, and provide experimentally testable scaling relations. The non-exponential decay patterns reveal fundamental limitations of Markovian approaches, and the framework guides the design of noise-resilient qubit architectures.
tldr: This paper models non-stationary decoherence in superconducting qubits using memory multi-fractional Brownian motion and a time-dependent Caldeira-Leggett environment, predicting stretched-exponential decay and non-Markovian dephasing.
motivation: Standard models of decoherence assume stationary noise, but experimental data often show time-dependent 1/f noise and long-range correlations. This work aims to capture such non-stationary effects to better understand and mitigate decoherence in superconducting qubits.
method: The authors extend their prior stochastic drift model (SdM) by introducing a time-dependent Hurst exponent H(t) and adaptive memory kernel K(t,s) for classical noise, and a time-dependent Caldeira-Leggett spectral density J(ω;t) with exponent s(t)=2H(t)-1 for the quantum bath. They derive an effective time-local Lindblad master equation and simulate qubit dynamics.
result: Key findings include: (1) relaxation and noise amplitudes independently affect energy decay; (2) time-varying H(t) matches experimental 1/f spectra better than constant exponents; (3) adaptive kernel preserves correlations without artificial damping; (4) predicted coherence times T1~5e6 ns, T2~4.18e5 ns under charge noise; and (5) stretched-exponential Ramsey and echo decay, non-Markovian dephasing, and a temperature-driven quantum-to-classical crossover.
conclusion: The framework reveals limitations of Markovian approaches and provides experimentally testable scaling relations, guiding the design of noise-resilient qubit architectures. Future work could extend to other qubit types and experimental verification.

title: A Risk-Aware Framework For Covert Quantum Communication Under Stochastic Channel Uncertainty
authors: Abbas Arghavani, Shahid Raza, Maryam Amiri, Alessandro Papadopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Covert quantum communication (CQC) seeks to hide not only message content but also the existence of communication. Existing CQC models usually assume deterministic or worst-case channel conditions, which are difficult to justify in realistic free-space optical and quantum links affected by turbulence, fluctuating background radiance, and stochastic detector noise. We propose a stochastic risk-aware optimization framework for CQC under uncertain physical-layer conditions. By modeling transmissivity and background noise as random variables, we express covertness and reliability guarantees through chance constraints with explicit outage budgets [MATH] and [MATH]. This recasts CQC design as a risk-calibrated resource-allocation problem balancing throughput, covertness, reliability, and communication privacy. We derive quantile-based reformulations of the outage constraints, characterize feasible operating regions under stochastic uncertainty, and introduce a complementary risk-adjusted utility formulation to expose throughput-risk trade-offs. The analysis reveals that modest relaxations in acceptable covertness-outage risk can yield large throughput gains, while aggressive optimization may break covertness outside sparse-transmission regimes. Monte Carlo results under log-normal fading and stochastic thermal noise show that the framework expands feasible operating regions, improves covert throughput by more than an order of magnitude, and identifies degradation boundaries beyond which covert operation becomes unreliable. These results move CQC closer to realistic secure quantum networking for free-space, satellite, and low-probability-of-detection applications.
tldr: A risk-aware optimization framework for covert quantum communication under stochastic channel uncertainty, using chance constraints to balance throughput, covertness, and reliability.
motivation: Existing CQC models assume deterministic or worst-case channel conditions, unrealistic for free-space and satellite links with turbulence and noise. A stochastic framework is needed to handle real-world uncertainties.
method: Model transmissivity and background noise as random variables; formulate covertness and reliability as chance constraints with outage budgets; derive quantile-based reformulations and a risk-adjusted utility function.
result: Modest relaxations in covertness-outage risk yield large throughput gains; the framework expands feasible operating regions and improves covert throughput by over an order of magnitude under log-normal fading and stochastic thermal noise.
conclusion: The framework moves CQC closer to practical deployment in free-space, satellite, and low-probability-of-detection quantum networks, highlighting trade-offs between risk and performance.

title: Scalable Single-Step Generation Of W States In 2d Superconducting Qubit Lattices
authors: Jo\~ao H. Romeiro, Federico A. Roy, Niklas Bruckmoser, Ivan Tsitsilin, Niklas J. Glaser, Christian M. F. Schneider, Gerhard B. P. Huber, Saya A. Sch\"obe, Johannes Schirk, Florian Wallner, Malay Singh, Julius Feigl, Leon Koch, Lasse S\"odergren, Max Werninghaus, Stefan Filipp
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reliable generation of multi-qubit entanglement is a prerequisite for large-scale quantum information technologies. In particular, W states are a valuable resource owing to their resilience under local loss or measurement. Nevertheless, preparing these states with sequential two-qubit gates often requires substantial time overhead. By contrast, engineered simultaneous interactions enable fast entanglement generation, even in qubit systems with limited nearest-neighbour connectivity. Here, we demonstrate a set of fast and robust operations for coherently distributing a single excitation across a lattice of arbitrary size, thereby directly generating W states from initial product states. In 2D lattices, the excitation propagates along both directions simultaneously, such that the total entanglement time scales only with the largest dimension. We exploit this property to prepare a six-qubit W state in a 3[MATH]2 superconducting lattice within 99 ns, achieving a tomographic fidelity of 83.9[MATH]1.0%. We then extend the protocol to create entanglement across chains of up to seven qubits, with the largest W state generated in 264 ns with a fidelity of 79.6[MATH]1.3%.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a fast, scalable method to generate multi-qubit W states in 2D superconducting qubit lattices using engineered simultaneous interactions, achieving high-fidelity entanglement in under 100 ns.
motivation: Efficient generation of multi-qubit entangled states like W states is crucial for quantum information technologies, but sequential two-qubit gates are slow. The authors aim to overcome this by using simultaneous interactions to speed up entanglement distribution.
method: The protocol uses engineered simultaneous interactions in a 2D superconducting qubit lattice to coherently distribute a single excitation, generating W states directly from product states. The excitation propagates along both dimensions, so the time scales with the largest dimension.
result: A six-qubit W state was prepared in a 3×2 lattice in 99 ns with 83.9% fidelity, and a seven-qubit chain W state in 264 ns with 79.6% fidelity.
conclusion: The method is scalable and fast, enabling W state generation in larger lattices with minimal time overhead, which is promising for quantum communication and networking applications.

title: Work To Insert A Particle Into An Active Fluid
authors: Freddy A. Cisneros, Alexandre Solon, Jordan M. Horowitz
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19026v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The chemical potential is defined as the work to quasi-statically add a particle to an equilibrium system. Inspired by this definition, we investigate how the work to add a particle to an active fluid depends on the activity, density, and insertion protocol. We find that the average work is protocol dependent and decreases with activity. Moreover, the work fluctuations retain asymmetric non-Gaussian tails even for slow particle insertions. We then compare the average particle-insertion work to the steady-state densities observed when two active fluids are brought into diffusive contact and observe opposing trends between density and work.
tldr: This paper extends the concept of chemical potential to active fluids, showing that the work to insert a particle is protocol-dependent and decreases with activity, with non-Gaussian fluctuations persisting even in the slow-insertion limit.
motivation: To understand how activity modifies the thermodynamic cost of adding a particle, inspired by the equilibrium definition of chemical potential.
method: Analytical and numerical calculations for a model active fluid (e.g., run-and-tumble particles) under different insertion protocols, analyzing average work and fluctuations.
result: Average insertion work decreases with activity and depends on protocol; work fluctuations retain asymmetric non-Gaussian tails even for slow insertions; comparison with diffusive contact shows opposing trends between density and work.
conclusion: The work to insert a particle in active fluids is not a state function, challenging equilibrium thermodynamic analogies; suggests new thermodynamic relations for active matter.

title: Quantum Koopman Algorithms
authors: David Jennings, Kamil Korzekwa, Matteo Lostaglio, Guoming Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19054v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define an observable-space framework of Quantum Koopman Algorithms (QKAs) for simulating the dynamics of both linear quantum and nonlinear classical systems, based on approximately closed sets of observables and efficient coherent encodings of their Koopman-driven evolution. QKAs have two strands: Dynamic-QKA for the initial-value problem of observables dynamics, and Spectral-QKA for the eigenvalue analysis of the Koopman operator. We demonstrate the scope of the framework through several applications. First, for classes of [MATH] free fermions linearly coupled to a bath, we construct quantum algorithms with gate cost [MATH], an exponential improvement over classical methods, and use them to reconstruct heat flows and decay rates. Second, for nonlinear classical dynamics, we introduce a novel nonlinear interaction-picture quantum algorithm that enables perturbative expansions around solvable nonlinear reference flows, going beyond existing approaches that only apply to weakly nonlinear systems. Third, we develop spectral methods for extracting eigen-frequencies of late-time nonlinear dynamics, introducing a windowed quantum ODE-solver. Our results identify the Koopman-quantum interface as a natural setting in which quantum algorithms can exploit observable-space structure to simulate both classical and quantum dynamics.
tldr: The paper introduces Quantum Koopman Algorithms for simulating quantum and classical dynamics, with applications to heat flows and decay rates in open quantum systems.
motivation: To develop efficient quantum algorithms for simulating dynamics of linear quantum and nonlinear classical systems by exploiting observable-space structure.
method: Defines an observable-space framework using Koopman operator theory, with two strands: Dynamic-QKA for initial-value problems and Spectral-QKA for eigenvalue analysis. Includes a nonlinear interaction-picture quantum algorithm for perturbative expansions.
result: Demonstrates exponential improvement in gate cost for simulating free fermions coupled to a bath, enabling reconstruction of heat flows and decay rates. Also provides spectral methods for extracting eigen-frequencies of nonlinear dynamics.
conclusion: The Koopman-quantum interface offers a natural setting for quantum algorithms to simulate both classical and quantum dynamics, with potential for further applications in thermodynamics and nonlinear systems.

title: Drive-Only Interaction Engineering Via Dynamical Freezing
authors: Songbo Xie, Jiheng Duan, Sabre Kais
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Freezing is usually used to suppress unwanted dynamics, but it can also be used to engineer interactions. We introduce freezing-induced interaction engineering, a drive-only control paradigm in which dynamically freezing an auxiliary subsystem reshapes the effective Hamiltonian of the remaining degrees of freedom. As a concrete realization, we consider a three-qubit architecture where a driven modulator [MATH] is coupled to one of two target qubits, [MATH], while [MATH] and [MATH] retain a fixed native exchange-type interaction. When [MATH] is frozen in a dressed eigenstate, its projection renormalizes the local Hamiltonian of [MATH]. This makes the dressed-frame detuning between [MATH] and [MATH] controllable by the drive frequency. The native interaction can then be switched between two regimes: an interaction-off regime with large dressed-frame detuning, and an interaction-on regime with resonant exchange. In the interaction-on regime, the protocol realizes an iSWAP gate using the native [MATH] coupling. Full lab-frame simulations show high-fidelity iSWAP dynamics and strong interaction suppression in the interaction-off regime. By combining native-coupling gate speed with drive-only operational simplicity, freezing-induced interaction engineering provides a route toward fast, drive-controlled entangling gates in fixed-frequency quantum architectures.
tldr: A drive-only control paradigm uses dynamical freezing of an auxiliary qubit to engineer effective interactions and realize high-fidelity iSWAP gates in fixed-frequency superconducting qubits.
motivation: To achieve fast, drive-controlled entangling gates without complex tunable couplers, leveraging freezing as a tool for interaction engineering rather than suppression.
method: The authors propose a three-qubit architecture where a driven modulator qubit is coupled to one target qubit; freezing the modulator in a dressed eigenstate renormalizes the target's Hamiltonian, making the dressed-frame detuning controllable by the drive frequency.
result: The native exchange interaction can be switched off (large detuning) or on (resonant exchange), realizing an iSWAP gate with high fidelity in full lab-frame simulations.
conclusion: This approach combines native-coupling gate speed with drive-only simplicity, offering a route toward fast entangling gates in fixed-frequency quantum architectures.

title: Rotational Quantum Tunneling Of A Magnetic Dipole In A Superconducting Trap
authors: Francis J. Headley, Fabian M\"uller, Emre K\"ose, Tim Fuchs, Hendrik Ulbricht, Daniel Braun
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the quantum dynamics of the rotational degree of freedom of a nano-magnet trapped in a superconducting trap. The nano-magnet is modeled as a magnetic dipole with magnetization pinned to the easy axis of the particle. The magnetic trap then leads to a potential barrier that hinders free rotation of the particle, but through which it can tunnel. We identified rest-gas scattering as the most important decoherence mechanism at low temperatures. A shape of the particle sufficiently close to perfect rotational symmetry about the rotational axis can protect the rotational tunneling against this decoherence mechanism, and we identify experimentally feasible parameter regimes where rotational tunneling should be observable.
tldr: This paper studies rotational quantum tunneling of a magnetic dipole in a superconducting trap, identifying decoherence mechanisms and parameter regimes for observability.
motivation: To understand the quantum dynamics of a nano-magnet's rotational degree of freedom in a superconducting trap, which is relevant for hybrid quantum systems and quantum sensing.
method: The nano-magnet is modeled as a magnetic dipole with magnetization pinned to its easy axis, and the trap creates a potential barrier. The study analyzes decoherence due to rest-gas scattering and the effect of particle shape symmetry.
result: Rest-gas scattering is the dominant decoherence mechanism at low temperatures, but a nearly perfect rotational symmetry about the rotation axis can protect tunneling. Experimentally feasible parameter regimes for observing rotational tunneling are identified.
conclusion: The findings suggest that rotational tunneling of a magnetic dipole in a superconducting trap is observable under realistic conditions, with implications for hybrid quantum systems and quantum information processing.

title: The Thermodynamic Costs Of Simple Linear Regression
authors: Samuel H. D'ambrosia, Sultan M. Daniels, Michael R. Deweese, Anant Sahai
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The construction of models from data is a significant contributor to the energetic costs of computation. Because of this, understanding how foundational thermodynamic bounds apply to modeling algorithms will be increasingly important. Here, we study the thermodynamic costs of a basic and fundamental modeling algorithm: simple linear regression. Following Landauer, we approximate the thermodynamic lower bound on irreversibly performing both exact linear regression and linear regression via stochastic gradient descent as implemented on floating-point numbers. From this, we derive energycost aware scaling laws for the optimal dataset size for training a linear regression model given a generalization error dependent demand for inference. Additionally, we discuss a method to lower bound the entropy production from the mismatch cost for algorithms with continuous input variables.
tldr: This paper derives thermodynamic lower bounds for simple linear regression and stochastic gradient descent, linking energy costs to dataset size and generalization error.
motivation: To understand the fundamental energetic costs of modeling algorithms, which are a significant contributor to computation energy consumption.
method: The authors approximate Landauer's bound for irreversible computation applied to floating-point implementations of exact linear regression and SGD, and derive energy-cost-aware scaling laws.
result: They obtain lower bounds on energy consumption for linear regression and scaling laws for optimal dataset size given a demand for inference accuracy.
conclusion: The work provides a framework for analyzing thermodynamic costs of machine learning algorithms, with implications for energy-efficient computing and further studies on mismatch cost for continuous variables.

title: Quantum Accreditation With Non-Clifford Two-qubit Gates
authors: Andrew Jackson, Theodoros Kapourniotis, Animesh Datta
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a family of quantum accreditation protocols for quantum circuits with non-Clifford two-qubit gates. The latter includes families of gates such as the fSim and XY families of gates, native to existing hardwares. We provide practical and scalable protocols that upper-bound the total variation distance between the probability distributions of error-free and erroneous quantum computations. We also establish the robustness of our protocols to small perturbations and generalize Pauli twirling to non-Pauli single-qubit bases, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: Develops accreditation protocols for quantum circuits with non-Clifford two-qubit gates, bounding the total variation distance between ideal and noisy distributions.
motivation: Existing accreditation protocols often assume Clifford gates, but many hardware-native gates (e.g., fSim, XY) are non-Clifford, requiring new methods to certify quantum computations.
method: Generalizes Pauli twirling to non-Pauli single-qubit bases and constructs scalable protocols that upper-bound the total variation distance between error-free and erroneous output distributions.
result: Provides practical, scalable accreditation protocols for non-Clifford two-qubit gates, with proven robustness to small perturbations.
conclusion: Enables reliable certification of quantum computations on current hardware, with potential extensions to other gate families and noise models.

title: Entangling Gate Performance And Fidelity Limits With Neutral Atom F\"orster Resonances
authors: S. A. Norrell, Y. Shen, M. Saffman, M. Otten
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neutral-atom entangling gates are commonly analyzed with a single effective Rydberg-pair state, but near F\"orster resonances the pair manifold contains resonantly coupled interaction channels that change both the control landscape and the achievable fidelity. We develop a two-eigenstate model for this regime and show that when allowing for coupling to both pair states in the resonance, the gate fidelity is bounded by [MATH], for interaction strength [MATH] and Rydberg lifetime [MATH]. We construct a gate protocol that saturates this bound in the large-Rabi-frequency limit, improving the existing fidelity limit by approximately [MATH]. We also evaluate common gate protocols near F\"orster resonances and find that retaining the exchange dynamics increases predicted fidelities by up to two orders of magnitude over earlier treatments.
tldr: This paper develops a two-eigenstate model for neutral-atom entangling gates near Förster resonances, deriving a fidelity bound and demonstrating improved gate performance by including exchange dynamics.
motivation: Neutral-atom entangling gates are typically analyzed with a single effective Rydberg-pair state, but near Förster resonances multiple interaction channels exist that affect fidelity. The authors aim to understand and improve gate fidelity in this regime.
method: The authors develop a two-eigenstate model that accounts for coupling to both pair states in the resonance, derive a fidelity bound, and construct a gate protocol that saturates this bound in the large-Rabi-frequency limit. They also evaluate common gate protocols near Förster resonances.
result: The gate fidelity is bounded by a function of interaction strength and Rydberg lifetime. The new protocol improves the existing fidelity limit by approximately a factor, and retaining exchange dynamics increases predicted fidelities by up to two orders of magnitude over earlier treatments.
conclusion: The work provides a more accurate model for neutral-atom gates near Förster resonances, leading to higher predicted fidelities and a protocol that approaches the fundamental limit. This has implications for quantum computing with neutral atoms.

title: Quantum Entanglement Halves The Oblivious Update Bandwidth
authors: Sagar Dubey
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider [MATH] MDS-coded distributed storage over [MATH] with per-node storage [MATH] symbols. For the oblivious update problem, where a single message symbol changes and neither helpers nor the stale node know which, the classical lower bound is [MATH] bits. We prove that when the [MATH] contacted helpers share prior quantum entanglement, the update bandwidth is [MATH] bits-equivalent, a factor approaching 2 reduction. For [MATH], a [MATH] CSS code achieves bandwidth [MATH] with one qudit per helper. For general [MATH], a [MATH] CSS code achieves the bound with [MATH] qudits per helper. The matching converse uses the superdense coding bound: the stale node holds all transmitted qudits and hence the entangled partners, so each helper's channel supports at most [MATH] distinguishable signals for dimension [MATH]. The result holds for all [MATH] pairs with sufficiently large prime [MATH].
tldr: Quantum entanglement halves the communication bandwidth required for oblivious updates in distributed storage systems.
motivation: To reduce the bandwidth overhead in distributed storage when a single symbol changes and no one knows which symbol changed, which is a fundamental problem in coding theory.
method: The authors use CSS codes and superdense coding to achieve a factor-of-2 reduction in update bandwidth, with a matching converse based on the superdense coding bound.
result: For MDS-coded distributed storage over a finite field, the update bandwidth can be reduced from the classical lower bound of 2 bits per symbol to 1 bit-equivalent per symbol using prior entanglement, approaching a factor of 2 reduction.
conclusion: The result demonstrates a clear quantum advantage in a practical distributed storage scenario, with implications for quantum networks and entanglement-assisted communication protocols.

title: A Review Of Galois Qudits
authors: Adam Wills
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18981v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Galois qudits are [MATH]-dimensional quantum systems whose choice of Pauli group encodes the arithmetic of some finite field [MATH]. They differ from the more familiar modular qudit, which are the same quantum system but whose choice of Pauli group are the clock and shift operators, which encode the arithmetic of integer addition and multiplication modulo [MATH]. Galois qudits are a useful mathematical construct that allow us to leverage the mathematical tools that are native to the larger qudit while only physically building smaller qudits. In particular, a Galois qudit of dimension [MATH] is exactly the same thing as a collection of [MATH] qubits, not only in its Hilbert space, but also in its Pauli group, and Clifford hierarchy. This formalism has found a lot of utility recently in constructing quantum error-correcting codes over qubits with useful properties. In this review, we build on existing literature to collect and formalise facts and proofs about Galois qudits over binary extension fields. We define them and their Clifford hierarchies, describe what it means to measure their Pauli operators, describe their stabiliser tableaux, formally define qudit-to-qubit mappings, and finally describe quantum Reed-Solomon codes.
tldr: This review formalizes Galois qudits over binary extension fields, showing they are equivalent to multiple qubits and enable construction of quantum error-correcting codes with useful properties.
motivation: Galois qudits provide a mathematical framework that leverages higher-dimensional structures while physically using qubits, offering advantages for quantum error correction and other protocols.
method: The paper collects and formalizes existing results, defining Galois qudits, their Pauli groups, Clifford hierarchies, stabilizer tableaux, and qudit-to-qubit mappings, with a focus on binary extension fields.
result: Key findings include a clear equivalence between Galois qudits of dimension 2^m and m qubits, and the construction of quantum Reed-Solomon codes with desirable properties.
conclusion: Galois qudits are a powerful tool for quantum error correction and may facilitate device-independent protocols and entanglement distillation, aligning with quantum communication interests.

title: Causal Fisher-Information Inequalities: Classical Causal Model Falsification And Metrological Advantage
authors: Su-Yong Lee Jeongho Bang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fisher-information inequalities have recently been used as operational witnesses of nonclassical metrological behavior, but their physical meaning is often tied to a particular narrative, such as, segmented dynamics or discrete trajectories. We show that a broader interpretation is available and, in fact, more natural: once an experiment is assumed to admit a classical causal model specified by a directed acyclic graph, conditional independences, and modular parameter dependence, the corresponding Fisher informations are forced to obey causal Fisher-information inequalities (CFIIs). The backbone result is a causal-path series law: for an additive causal parameter that propagates through a classical path [MATH], the inverse Fisher information behaves as an information resistance and must add in series. Consequently, any CFII violation is a rigorous falsification of the entire classical causal model class. We then show that the violation is automatically a metrological resource certificate, because it implies a precision that no member of the classical causal class can attain. The gain mechanism is identified as Fisher-information synergy, i.e. off-diagonal score correlations that classical modularity forbids. A single-qubit coherent-rotation example demonstrates the deterministic CFII violation, estimator-level achievability of the resulting gain, robustness against split-optimized classical benchmarks, and a chain-amplified advantage in long causal decompositions. Finally, an AI-assisted adversarial finite-data stress test shows that the witness remains certifiable under the realistic visibility loss and readout error, while optimized modular classical causal models saturate but do not cross the CFII frontier.
tldr: The paper introduces causal Fisher-information inequalities (CFIIs) that falsify classical causal models and certify metrological advantage via Fisher-information synergy.
motivation: To provide a general framework for using Fisher-information inequalities as operational witnesses of nonclassical metrological behavior, beyond specific narratives like segmented dynamics.
method: The authors derive a causal-path series law for additive parameters in classical causal models, showing that inverse Fisher information adds in series. They then demonstrate CFII violation in a single-qubit coherent rotation example and test robustness with AI-assisted adversarial finite-data stress tests.
result: CFII violation rigorously falsifies the entire classical causal model class and automatically certifies a metrological resource. The gain mechanism is Fisher-information synergy from off-diagonal score correlations forbidden in classical models.
conclusion: CFIIs provide a powerful tool for certifying quantum metrological advantage and falsifying classical causal explanations, with potential applications in quantum information and foundations.

title: Non-perturbative Measurements Of Two-point Functions In Quantum Field Theory
authors: T. Rick Perche Sebastian Holm\'en
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18945v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a non-perturbative method through which local probes can access the two-point function of a quantum field within a region of spacetime. By considering a lattice of gapless particle detectors, we identified the probe observables that encode the field's two-point function. We quantify the discrepancies introduced by physical finite-sized interaction regions by performing a spacetime multipole expansion of the smeared two-point function. Our protocol expresses the two-point function entirely in terms of measurable detectors correlations, providing an operational notion of states in QFT.
tldr: A non-perturbative method using a lattice of gapless detectors to measure the two-point function of a quantum field, providing an operational definition of field states.
motivation: To develop a measurement scheme for quantum field two-point functions that does not rely on perturbation theory, enabling direct experimental access to field correlations.
method: A lattice of gapless particle detectors is used to probe the field; the two-point function is extracted from detector correlations via a spacetime multipole expansion to account for finite-size effects.
result: The two-point function can be expressed entirely in terms of measurable detector correlations, with quantified discrepancies from finite interaction regions.
conclusion: This provides an operational notion of states in QFT and opens avenues for experimental tests of quantum field theory predictions.

title: Signatures Of Quantum Noise In The Operation Of Deutsch's Algorithm
authors: Katarzyna Roszak Ma{\l}gorzata Strza{\l}ka
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use Deutsch's algorithm as a stand in for more complex quantum algorithms in order to determine how quantum properties of an environment manifest themselves in results that can be obtained on quantum computers. We model pure dephasing in two different ways; one keeps the full density matrix of the qubits and environments (quantum) while the other uses Kraus operators (classical). We find that a single run of the algorithm yields the same effect in both cases, but running the algorithm twice leads to stark differences. Taking correlations and interplay between different decoherence processes into account leads to a slowing of decoherence effects for balanced functions. For constant functions, the effect is much more pronounced, and there is a qualitative change in the dependence of measurement outcomes on decoherence. We present results obtained on one of the IBM Quantum processors, which fully reproduce the predicted effect regardless of the assumptions made in the derivation. We further illustrate the findings on NV center spin qubits, which show more complex behavior due to a small size of the environment.
tldr: This paper uses Deutsch's algorithm to study how quantum vs classical noise models affect algorithm outcomes, revealing qualitative differences in multi-run decoherence effects.
motivation: To understand how quantum properties of an environment manifest in quantum algorithm results, using Deutsch's algorithm as a proxy for more complex algorithms.
method: Model pure dephasing via two approaches: full density matrix (quantum) and Kraus operators (classical); compare single and double runs; test on IBM Q and NV center spin qubits.
result: Single runs show identical effects for both models, but double runs reveal stark differences; correlations between decoherence processes slow decoherence for balanced functions and cause qualitative changes for constant functions.
conclusion: Quantum noise signatures can be detected in multi-run experiments, with implications for understanding decoherence in quantum computing and designing noise-resilient algorithms.

title: Quantum Magic Reveals Cp Phases Invisible To Entanglement In Spin-0 Decays
authors: Nicolas Viaux, Ariel Norambuena, Pedro Orellana
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: All standard scalar quantum-information measures -- concurrence, negativity, entanglement entropy, the optimized CHSH bound, and quantum Fisher information -- are CP-blind in ideal \\ spin-0 [MATH] decays because the two-qubit spin state is maximally entangled for every CP angle. motivation: Standard quantum information measures like concurrence and entanglement entropy are CP-blind in ideal spin-0 decays because the two-qubit spin state is maximally entangled for every CP angle. The authors sought a measure that could reveal CP phases in such systems.
method: The authors compute the stabilizer Rényi entropy in the physical Pauli frame of spin analysis, deriving an exact closed form. They then construct two experimentally accessible CP witnesses based on magic, comparing their statistical efficiencies.

title: Ancilla Assisted Quantum Process Tomography Using Bound Entangled States
authors: Gurvir Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lu [Ann. Phys. (Berlin) , 2100550 (2022)] posed the question of whether bound entangled states can be used for ancilla-assisted quantum process tomography (AAQPT). In this work, we answer this question in the affirmative by explicitly demonstrating that certain bound entangled states can be used for AAQPT. We further show that, although local filtering operations may improve the trace norm of the realignment criterion, they are essentially ineffective for AAQPT, as they render the resulting states and therefore unsuitable for reliable process reconstruction. Further, we investigate the efficiency of bound entangled states for AAQPT and establish quantitative bounds by comparing their performance with Werner and isotropic states. Our results therefore provide a new application of bound entangled states in the context of ancilla-assisted quantum process tomography.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that bound entangled states can be used for ancilla-assisted quantum process tomography, providing a new application for such states.
motivation: To answer whether bound entangled states, which are not distillable, can still be useful for quantum process tomography, a question posed by Lu (2022).
method: The authors explicitly construct bound entangled states and test their efficacy for AAQPT, comparing performance with Werner and isotropic states, and also examine the effect of local filtering operations.
result: Certain bound entangled states are indeed suitable for AAQPT, but local filtering operations are ineffective as they render the states unsuitable for reliable process reconstruction.
conclusion: Bound entangled states have a new application in quantum process tomography, and the work establishes quantitative bounds on their efficiency, suggesting further exploration of their utility in quantum information tasks.

title: Subsystem Relaxation And A Calibrated Sampling Diagnostic For Programmable Quantum Annealers
authors: Luis Lozano
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable quantum annealers are used as open-system samplers, but it is unclear when reverse annealing erases preparation memory and what the readout represents. Here we implement a subsystem-environment protocol on two D-Wave quantum annealers, varying environment size, coupling, disorder, preparation, geometry and QPU generation. A six-qubit subsystem becomes initial-state independent when the environment is large or strongly coupled, while quenched disorder and atypical environment states arrest relaxation. Pairing the memory order parameter with the distance to a calibrated conditional-Boltzmann reference yields a diagnostic that flags rare wrong-basin trapping memory loss alone misses; memory-retaining conditions stay far from the reference (median 0.35). Relaxed ferromagnetic readouts are near-deterministic, so small distances there are a consistency check, not a thermometric test. In a mixed-frustration benchmark, the local-update model practitioners assume mispredicts QPU relaxation roughly sevenfold, whereas non-local classical sampling recovers it. We provide a subsystem-level validation protocol for quantum-annealer sampling.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies subsystem relaxation in D-Wave quantum annealers, introducing a diagnostic to detect memory loss and wrong-basin trapping, and finds that non-local classical sampling better reproduces QPU relaxation than the local-update model.
motivation: To understand when reverse annealing erases preparation memory and what the readout represents in programmable quantum annealers, which is crucial for their use as open-system samplers.
method: A subsystem-environment protocol is implemented on two D-Wave quantum annealers, varying environment size, coupling, disorder, preparation, geometry, and QPU generation. A memory order parameter and distance to a calibrated conditional-Boltzmann reference are used as diagnostics.
result: A six-qubit subsystem becomes initial-state independent when the environment is large or strongly coupled; quenched disorder and atypical environment states arrest relaxation. The diagnostic flags rare wrong-basin trapping that memory loss alone misses. Non-local classical sampling recovers QPU relaxation, while the local-update model mispredicts it roughly sevenfold.
conclusion: The work provides a subsystem-level validation protocol for quantum-annealer sampling, highlighting the need for non-local classical models and offering a diagnostic for reliable sampling.

title: Statistical Quantum Phase Estimation: Extensions And Practical Considerations
authors: Brandon Allen Amit Surana
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present several refinements and extensions of the statistical quantum phase estimation (SQPE) framework to address some of its key practical limitations, improving its applicability to realistic cases. Recently, a family of statistical approaches for QPE have been proposed where each run uses only a few ancillae and shorter circuits than standard QPE and thus is better suited for early fault-tolerant quantum computers that are qubit-and depth-limited. SQPE method within that family estimates the cumulative distribution function (CDF) associated with spectral density of the Hamiltonian for a given trial state by using its Fourier approximation and then identifies the first jump discontinuity of the CDF to determine the ground state energy (GSE) of the Hamiltonian. It relies on random compilation procedure based on linear combination of unitaries (LCU) decomposition of the Hamiltonian assuming positive Pauli weights and requires a good estimate of lower bound on the overlap between the trial and true ground state, both of which may be difficult to achieve in practice. We address these limitations by generalizing the random compilation procedure for negative Pauli weights and employing a changepoint detection method for determining GSE which does not rely on an estimate of this overlap. We also show that by exploiting symmetry of the Fourier series one can reduce number of circuit runs/samples by a factor of 2x while keeping the GSE estimation accuracy the same. We illustrate these new developments numerically via a quantum simulator in Qiskit.
tldr: This paper extends the statistical quantum phase estimation framework to handle negative Pauli weights and removes the need for overlap estimates, improving practical applicability for early fault-tolerant quantum computers.
motivation: Standard SQPE requires positive Pauli weights and a good estimate of the overlap between trial and ground state, which are often impractical. The authors aim to remove these limitations to make SQPE more broadly applicable.
method: They generalize the random compilation procedure to allow negative Pauli weights and use a changepoint detection method to identify the ground state energy without needing overlap estimates. They also exploit Fourier series symmetry to halve the number of circuit runs.
result: The generalized SQPE works with negative Pauli weights, does not require overlap estimates, and achieves a 2x reduction in samples while maintaining accuracy. Numerical simulations in Qiskit validate the approach.
conclusion: These refinements make SQPE more practical for early fault-tolerant quantum computers, potentially reducing resource requirements for ground state energy estimation. Future work could explore further optimizations or applications to other problems.

title: 4d And 5d Layer Codes Through Color Routing
authors: Nou\'edyn Baspin Andrew C. Yuan

title: Noise-induced Simulability Transition From Operator Scrambling
authors: Neil Dowling, Xhek Turkeshi, Jacopo de Nardis, Guglielmo Lami
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The complexity of simulating quantum many-body dynamics, or quantum computations, in the Heisenberg picture is governed by the scrambling of initially simple operators into superpositions of exponentially many Pauli strings. The corresponding expansion coefficients define the Pauli spectrum, whose structure controls the performance of classical algorithms based on truncating Pauli expansions. Here we determine the finite-depth Pauli spectrum of random quantum circuits, both in the noiseless case and in the presence of local noise, through its moments, given by the operator stabilizer R\'enyi entropies. In noiseless circuits, we uncover a hierarchy in the approach to the fully scrambled regime: low moments equilibrate at relatively short depths, while higher moments, which are sensitive to rare, large-amplitude Pauli coefficients, require parametrically larger depths. In noisy circuits, scrambling competes with an effective suppression of operator spreading. Above a critical error per cycle [MATH], the operator fails to reach the fully scrambled distribution and remains supported on an atypically sparse subset of Pauli strings. Conversely, below this scale, we rigorously show that classical simulation remains exponentially hard, demonstrating that finite noise does not automatically imply classical simulability. The resulting noise-induced transition in operator complexity therefore delineates the boundary between intrinsically hard quantum dynamics and those that remain classically accessible.
tldr: This paper studies the Pauli spectrum of random quantum circuits and shows a noise-induced transition in operator complexity that determines classical simulability.
motivation: To understand how noise affects the complexity of simulating quantum dynamics in the Heisenberg picture, and to identify conditions under which classical simulation becomes tractable.
method: The authors analyze the moments of the Pauli spectrum (operator stabilizer Rényi entropies) for random quantum circuits with and without local noise, deriving critical error thresholds.
result: In noiseless circuits, low moments equilibrate faster than high moments. In noisy circuits, above a critical error rate the operator fails to scramble fully, but below that rate classical simulation remains exponentially hard.
conclusion: Finite noise does not automatically imply classical simulability; there is a sharp transition that separates hard quantum dynamics from classically accessible ones.

title: Non-Gaussianity Of Random Quantum States
authors: Filiberto Ares, Sara Murciano, Pasquale Calabrese

title: Operator-Algebraic Methods For Asymptotic-Preserving Quantum Simulation Of Open Systems
authors: M. W. Almasri
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a mathematically rigorous framework for simulating using quantum computational resources, by translating the into the formalism of quantum channels and Lindbladian dynamics. For stiff open quantum systems governed by singularly perturbed generators [MATH] with [MATH], we prove that layered quantum protocols, which implement fast-scale relaxation via native analog evolution or analytic manifold projection, converge uniformly in the diamond norm to consistent discretizations of the limiting slow dynamics, with explicit error bound [MATH] independent of stiffness. title: Logical Resource Estimation For Quantum State Preparation With Compilation
authors: Diyi Liu, Hanyu Wang, Shuchen Zhu, Jason Cong, Wibe A. de Jong, Di Fang, Zhen Huang, Costin Iancu, Chao Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum state preparation is a fundamental primitive in quantum algorithms for encoding classical data into quantum amplitudes. We compare the cost of preparing general [MATH]-qubit states with real amplitudes using two common paradigms: rotation-based methods, based on controlled rotations, and sampling-based methods, based on a structured representation of the target state. Although these approaches are often theoretically compared using CNOT count and [MATH]-count, their relative performance in total gate count remains less well understood practically. We compare representative rotation-based and sampling-based methods using [MATH]-count and total gate count, and analyze how compilation overhead affects their relative performance. We also develop a software package for compiling state preparation circuits, designed as a practical subroutine for more general quantum computations. result: Sampling-based methods achieve asymptotically lower T-count and retain an overall advantage after accounting for total gate count and compilation overhead.
conclusion: Sampling-based methods are more efficient for preparing general n-qubit states with real amplitudes, and the developed software package can serve as a practical subroutine for larger quantum computations.

title: Spectral Geometric Mean And Trace Characterizations

title: Clifford Symmetries In Quantum Many-body Systems
authors: Charlie Nation, Rick P. A. Simon, Shreya Banerjee, Francesco Martini, Alessandro Ricottone, Federico Cerisola, Luca Dellantonio
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Obtaining the symmetries of a model is a critical step towards developing an understanding and ultimately analytically or numerically solving the model. However, finding symmetries is generally extremely complicated, often being the result of insightful thinking. In this work, we complement human ingenuity with an algorithm. We leverage the classically efficient Clifford group to find symmetries for arbitrary many-body Hamiltonians via a graph representation. We demonstrate our method on random and physical Hamiltonians, with instances of up to one thousand qubits and demonstrate how our approach can provide deeper understanding of the model.
tldr: This paper uses Clifford group symmetries to find symmetries in many-body Hamiltonians via a graph representation, demonstrated on up to 1000 qubits.
motivation: Finding symmetries in quantum many-body models is crucial for understanding and solving them, but is typically difficult and relies on human insight.
method: The authors leverage the classically efficient Clifford group and a graph representation to algorithmically discover symmetries in arbitrary many-body Hamiltonians.
result: The method successfully identifies symmetries in random and physical Hamiltonians, scaling to systems of up to 1000 qubits.
conclusion: The approach provides a systematic way to uncover symmetries, potentially aiding in deeper understanding of quantum models, though its direct application to the user's specific interests is limited.

title: Efficient Fourier-Based Linear Combination Of Unitaries And Applications In Quantum Optimization
authors: Almudena Carrera Vazquez, Daniel J. Egger, Stefan Woerner
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate ancilla-free linear combination of unitaries (LCU) as a framework for approximating complex quantum circuits. This is particularly effective for quantum optimization algorithms, where candidate solutions can be evaluated classically and the task is to sample high-quality bitstrings rather than reproduce the full output distribution. We show that Fourier-based LCU constructions efficiently decompose broad classes of diagonal and non-diagonal unitaries, replacing highly connected qubit interactions with single-qubit gate layers or significantly simpler structures at the cost of a polynomial sampling overhead. Applied to algorithms such as QAOA, this yields efficient, hardware-friendly decompositions of, for instance, cardinality-constraint penalties and the fully connected XY-mixer, while maintaining rigorous performance guarantees compared to fully coherent implementations. Furthermore, we establish a formal connection between Fourier-based quantum penalties and Lagrangian relaxation, offering a unified perspective on constraint handling. We validate our approach using exact statevector simulations of 12-qubit circuits and large-scale experiments on 106 superconducting qubits. Our results illustrate how approximate sampling via an LCU systematically trades circuit complexity for sampling overhead, extending the practical reach of near-term quantum optimization.
tldr: This paper proposes Fourier-based ancilla-free LCU decompositions to simplify quantum circuits for optimization, trading circuit depth for sampling overhead.
motivation: To reduce hardware requirements for near-term quantum optimization algorithms like QAOA by replacing complex interactions with simpler gates.
method: Fourier-based linear combination of unitaries (LCU) to decompose diagonal and non-diagonal unitaries into single-qubit gates and simpler structures, with polynomial sampling overhead.
result: Efficient decompositions for cardinality-constraint penalties and fully connected XY-mixer, validated on 12-qubit simulations and 106-qubit experiments.
conclusion: Approximate sampling via LCU systematically trades circuit complexity for sampling overhead, extending the reach of near-term quantum optimization.

title: Achieving High Filling Of An Optical Lattice By Light-Assisted Redistribution Of Atoms
authors: Lauren Weiss, Evan Yamaguchi, Claire Pritts, Tadej Me\v{z}nar\v{s}i\v{c}, Cheng Chin
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable arrays of individual atoms provide an ideal starting point for quantum information and simulation experiments. However, their preparation is often limited by light-assisted collisions (LACs), which typically result in parity-projected filling fractions of [MATH]. In this work we demonstrate a light-assisted redistribution process in the Quantum Matter Synthesizer that overcomes this constraint by stochastically moving atoms from multiply occupied lattice sites to neighboring vacant sites. Using a blue-detuned optical pumping beam during degenerate Raman sideband cooling, we achieve single-atom filling fractions of [MATH]. We find that over 50[MATH] of the atoms involved in radiative collisions are retained in the lattice. The redistribution process involves many LACs over an extended time as atoms diffuse to empty sites. Our demonstration offers a scalable and efficient pathway toward unity-filled atom arrays without the need for complex rearrangement protocols, with broad applicability to quantum simulation, precision measurements, and quantum information control.

motivation: Scalable arrays of individual atoms are crucial for quantum information and simulation, but preparation is limited by light-assisted collisions that typically yield only parity-projected filling fractions.
method: The authors use a blue-detuned optical pumping beam during degenerate Raman sideband cooling to stochastically move atoms from multiply occupied sites to neighboring vacant sites in a Quantum Matter Synthesizer.

title: Floquet-Engineered Odd-Parity Altermagnetic Higher-Order Topology In A Two-Dimensional Antiferromagnet Cr$_2$CH$_2$
authors: Xiaorong Zou, Hyeon Suk Shin, Baibiao Huang, Yanmei Zang, Ying Dai, Chengwang Niu, Chang-Jong Kang, Chang Woo Myung
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Periodic driving provides a platform to dynamically tailor quantum states of matter, yet its impact on symmetry-protected topological phases remains incompletely understood. Here, we demonstrate that periodic driving enables the realization of an odd-parity altermagnetic (AM) higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) phase in the Cr[MATH]CH[MATH] monolayer. In equilibrium, Cr[MATH]CH[MATH] is a 2D antiferromagnetic (AFM) HOTI protected by [MATH] rotational symmetry, characterized by a symmetry indicator [MATH] = [MATH] and robust corner states. title: Implementation Of Finite State Logic Machines Via The Dynamics Of Atomic Systems
authors: Dawit Hiluf Hailu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Following the success of Moore's predictions, we are approaching a limit in the miniaturization of semiconductors for computing materials. This has led to the exploration of various research paths to develop alternative computing paradigms, such as quantum computing, 3D transistors, molecular logic, and continuous logic. In this context, we propose a novel approach in which the dynamics of a two-level atom is used to execute classical Boolean logic operations. Unlike traditional combinational logic circuits, where the output depends solely on the input, we suggest a finite-state machine-like computing model, where the output is influenced by both the input and the system's initial state. The proposed mechanism leverages the dynamics of a two-level quantum state, with information encoded in observable quantities. These observables, the density matrix's population (diagonal) and coherence (off-diagonal) elements, were analyzed using the Liouville equation. The selection of observables within the Liouville space allows us to encode more variables. Although environmental noise may cause some loss of encoded information, fast computations can still be performed before it dissipates. In addition, logic operations can be read in parallel, enabling complex computations. This system can also be scaled to an N-level configuration.
tldr: The paper proposes using the dynamics of a two-level atom to implement finite-state logic machines, leveraging quantum observables for classical Boolean operations.
motivation: To explore alternative computing paradigms beyond traditional semiconductor miniaturization, specifically using atomic dynamics for logic operations.
method: The authors model a two-level quantum system using the Liouville equation, encoding information in population and coherence elements of the density matrix, and analyze how these observables can represent finite-state machine logic.
result: The approach demonstrates that Boolean logic operations can be executed via atomic dynamics, with the output depending on both input and initial state, enabling parallel readout and scalability to N-level systems.
conclusion: The work suggests a novel computing model but acknowledges environmental noise as a challenge; fast computations before decoherence are possible, and scaling to multi-level systems is feasible.

title: Finite-temperature Crossover From Coherent Magnons To Energy Superdiffusion In The Pxp Model
authors: Shengtao Jiang, Jean-Yves Desaules, Marko Ljubotina, Thomas Scaffidi
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The PXP chain was recently shown to exhibit superdiffusive energy transport with Kardar-Parisi-Zhang-like scaling, [MATH], joining a growing number of spin chains with this exponent. title: Translation-invariant Quantum Low-density Parity-check Codes From Compactified Fracton Models
authors: Cassandra M. Hopkin, Victor V. Albert, Dominic J. Williamson
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum error-correcting codes with translation symmetry and local checks have been studied extensively, leading to a wide variety of fracton codes in three or more dimensions which lack a complete unifying picture. Recently, the study of translation-invariant codes with long-range checks has revealed impressive performance for small fixed-size instances in two dimensions. Here, we provide a unifying picture for a large family of translation-invariant codes, both local and long-range, that captures many fracton codes and all Abelian Two-Block Group Algebra (A2BGA) codes, including the Bivariate Bicycle (BB) codes. The balanced product structure of A2BGA codes leads to a local parent code that is a hypergraph product fracton model in a higher dimension. Different compactifications of a parent code produce a wide variety of descendant codes which provides a unifying picture for their properties. In particular, all BB codes with the same check weight are derived from a single parent hypergraph product fracton model. This construction allows us to extend Wang and Pryadko's code-parameter bounds for Generalized Bicycle codes to A2BGA codes. We conjecture that the transversal gates and energy barriers of the translation-invariant descendant codes are limited by those of their parent fracton models.
tldr: This paper unifies translation-invariant quantum LDPC codes, including fracton and A2BGA codes, via a balanced product construction and compactification of higher-dimensional parent codes.
motivation: To provide a unifying framework for translation-invariant quantum codes with local or long-range checks, and to extend known parameter bounds to a broader class of codes.
method: The authors use the balanced product structure of A2BGA codes to construct a local parent hypergraph product fracton model in higher dimensions, then compactify it to obtain descendant codes.
result: All BB codes with the same check weight derive from a single parent fracton model; code-parameter bounds for generalized bicycle codes are extended to A2BGA codes.
conclusion: The work suggests that transversal gates and energy barriers of descendant codes are limited by those of parent fracton models, offering a path to understand code properties.

title: Variational Diffusion Channel Decoder
authors: Chengwei Zhang, Yifan Du, Siyu Liao
abstract: ArXiv:2605.18902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Neural channel decoder, as a data-driven channel decoding strategy, has shown very promising improvement on error-correcting capability over the classical methods. However, the success of those deep learning-based decoder comes at the cost of drastically increased model storage and computational complexity, hindering their practical adoptions in real-world time-sensitive resource-sensitive communication and storage systems. To address this challenge, we propose an efficient variational diffusion model-based channel decoder, which effectively integrates the domain-specific belief propagation process to the modern diffusion model. By reaping the low-cost benefits of belief propagation and strong learning capability of diffusion model, our proposed neural decoder simultaneously achieves very low cost and high error-correcting performance. Experimental results show that, compared with the state-of-the-art neural channel decoders, our model provides a feasible solution for practical deployment via achieving the best decoding performance with significantly reduced computational cost and model size.
tldr: The paper proposes a variational diffusion model-based channel decoder that integrates belief propagation to achieve low-cost, high-performance error correction.
motivation: Deep learning-based neural channel decoders suffer from high model storage and computational complexity, hindering practical deployment in time- and resource-sensitive communication systems.
method: The authors combine a variational diffusion model with belief propagation, leveraging the low cost of belief propagation and the learning capability of diffusion models to design an efficient decoder.
result: The proposed decoder achieves the best decoding performance with significantly reduced computational cost and model size compared to state-of-the-art neural channel decoders.
conclusion: The work provides a feasible solution for practical deployment of neural decoders, but its relevance to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics is minimal.

title: Most Probable Kam Tori In Stochastic Hamiltonian Systems Driven By Multiplicative Noise
authors: Yong Li Xinze Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19292v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates the effect of random perturbations, in particular multiplicative noise, on the integrable structure of Hamiltonian systems, with a particular focus on KAM theory for stochastic Hamiltonian dynamics. We prove that, under suitable assumptions, for an integrable Hamiltonian system subject to both a small deterministic perturbation and multiplicative noise, the invariant tori with Diophantine frequencies persist in the sense of most probable paths. Furthermore, when the intensity of the multiplicative noise is sufficiently small, we use the large deviation principle to characterize the asymptotic probability of solution trajectories deviating from these invariant tori, and we derive the corresponding rate function.
tldr: This paper studies the persistence of KAM tori in stochastic Hamiltonian systems with multiplicative noise, using large deviation principles to characterize deviations.
motivation: To understand how random perturbations affect the integrable structure of Hamiltonian systems, extending KAM theory to stochastic settings.
method: The authors prove persistence of invariant tori in the sense of most probable paths under small deterministic and multiplicative noise perturbations, and apply large deviation theory to estimate deviation probabilities.
result: Invariant tori with Diophantine frequencies persist as most probable paths, and the asymptotic probability of deviations is characterized by a rate function when noise intensity is small.
conclusion: The work provides a stochastic extension of KAM theory, with potential implications for understanding stability in noisy Hamiltonian systems, but direct applications to the user's interests are limited.

title: Soft Covering Through The Lens Of Hypothesis Testing
authors: Neri Merhav
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the soft covering phenomenon through the lens of Neyman--Pearson hypothesis testing: given a channel output sequence [MATH], can one decide whether it was produced when the channel was driven by a random codeword, or generated independently from the output marginal? We derive exact exponential decay rates for the jointly averaged false-alarm (FA) probability [MATH] and missed-detection (MD) probability [MATH], as functions of the decision threshold [MATH] and the codebook rate [MATH]. The derived single-letter formulas of the exponents [MATH] and [MATH] are tight in the random coding sense. The analysis reveals a rich phase structure. For [MATH], there is a genuine exponential tradeoff between the two error types over the interval [MATH]. At [MATH], this tradeoff interval collapses to the single point [MATH], where both error exponents simultaneously vanish, a fact which manifests the soft covering phenomenon in the Neyman--Pearson sense. For [MATH], the same instantaneous collapse persists at [MATH]; moreover, for every [MATH] at least one exponent is zero: the FA exponent is zero for [MATH] (FA probability does not decay exponentially), and the MD exponent is zero for [MATH] (and finite, channel-specific for [MATH]; see Remark~). There is no interval of [MATH] where both exponents are simultaneously positive. A sharp phase transition in the MD exponent occurs at [MATH] for all rates.
tldr: This paper analyzes the soft covering phenomenon in information theory using Neyman-Pearson hypothesis testing, deriving exact error exponents for false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities.
motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of distinguishing between a channel output generated by a random codeword versus an independent output, which is relevant to information-theoretic security and channel coding.
method: The authors use large deviations theory and random coding to derive single-letter formulas for the exponential decay rates of false-alarm and missed-detection probabilities as functions of the decision threshold and codebook rate.
result: They find a rich phase structure: for rates below capacity, there is a tradeoff interval where both error exponents are positive; at capacity, the interval collapses to a single point where both exponents vanish; for rates above capacity, at least one exponent is zero, with a sharp phase transition in the missed-detection exponent.
conclusion: The results provide a complete characterization of the soft covering phenomenon in the Neyman-Pearson sense, with implications for hypothesis testing and channel coding, but the paper is primarily theoretical and not directly connected to the user's research interests.

title: Revisiting Recursive Methods For Dyson And Keldysh In Negf: Part I
authors: Edoardo Di Napoli, Alessandro Pecchia, Gustavo Ramirez-Hidalgo
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The simulation of quantum transport in nanodevices requires the solution of the Dyson and Keldysh equations, a task dominated by the inversion of massive, block-tridiagonal matrices. While the Recursive Green's Function (RGF) method has long been the standard [MATH] solver for quasi-1D systems, its formulation has typically been restricted to sequential execution and nearest-neighbor interactions. In this work, we carefully reformulate RGF through the lens of Domain Decomposition and Schur Complement theory. This allows us to extend the recursive formalism to block [MATH]-diagonal systems (handling higher-order stencils) and to derive a parallel algorithm, Domain-Decomposition based RGF (DDRGF), which stitches macroscopic domains via reduced interface systems. We explore data dependencies in DDRGF in detail, by means of block-sparse structures and tracing back to the desired output as a block tridiagonal approximation, giving a clear, reproducible and extensible formulation. We validate these algorithms using , a Julia-based implementation, demonstrating that the structural insights of domain decomposition provide a robust pathway for high-performance quantum transport simulations on modern multi-core clusters. The theory presented here lays down the base for tackling the Keldysh problem, to be similarly handled in future stages of our work. Although the target here is the acceleration of kernels in the non-equilibrium Green's function method, the algorithms and the implementations presented can be immediately used in any application involving block [MATH]-diagonal systems.
tldr: This paper reformulates the Recursive Green's Function method using domain decomposition and Schur complements to enable parallel computation and handle higher-order stencils for quantum transport simulations.
motivation: To accelerate the solution of Dyson and Keldysh equations in NEGF for nanodevices, which currently relies on sequential RGF methods limited to nearest-neighbor interactions.
method: The authors apply domain decomposition and Schur complement theory to extend RGF to block k-diagonal systems and derive a parallel algorithm (DDRGF) that stitches macroscopic domains via reduced interface systems.
result: They validate the algorithm with a Julia implementation, demonstrating that domain decomposition provides a robust pathway for high-performance quantum transport simulations on multi-core clusters.
conclusion: The work lays the foundation for tackling the Keldysh problem in future stages and can be applied to any block k-diagonal system beyond quantum transport.

title: Embodying Intelligence Into Mechanical Metamaterials Via Reservoir Computing
authors: Shan He, Steven Kiyabu, Philip R. Buskohl, Patrick Musgrave
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study harnesses the embodied intelligence of mechanical metamaterials to sense and process environmental vibrations with minimal digital computation. Using physical reservoir computing (PRC), we turn the metamaterial and its nonlinear dynamics into a physical neural network that nonlinearly transforms the input vibrations and uses a simple linear training to compute a range of tasks. We introduce a novel metamaterial reservoir composed of a network of unit cells with contact nonlinearities that are the physical equivalent of leaky rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation functions. We experimentally show that the metamaterial reservoir can compute two classes of tasks: independent tasks, such as benchmark functions, and embodied tasks, such as proprioception, which we introduce to describe tasks coupled to the structure's dynamics. By comparing against a linear metamaterial, we demonstrate that nonlinearity is critical for high task performance, and we show that the metamaterial is robust to inputs of varying complexity. Through dimensionality reduction, we uncover the governing information separation mechanism and show that the metamaterial separates the input vibrations into new frequency content spatially distributed across the sensor readouts. We then confirm that frequency content is a key indicator of task performance by conducting an optimal sensor selection study using a frequency-based greedy algorithm. Finally, we demonstrate that a metamaterial's generalized performance for different tasks can be quantified using the memory vs. nonlinearity subspace, providing a design tool for other reservoir abstractions. These results establish the embodied intelligence of mechanical metamaterials and provide a path for sense-assess-response in intelligent systems.
tldr: This paper uses mechanical metamaterials as physical reservoir computers to process vibrations with minimal digital computation.
motivation: To harness embodied intelligence in mechanical metamaterials for sensing and processing environmental vibrations without extensive digital computation.
method: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) is implemented using a metamaterial with unit cells that have contact nonlinearities acting as leaky ReLU activation functions; linear readout training is applied.
result: The metamaterial reservoir performs benchmark tasks and embodied tasks like proprioception, with nonlinearity critical for performance; frequency content separation is identified as the key mechanism.
conclusion: The work establishes a design tool for reservoir computing in metamaterials, enabling sense-assess-response systems with minimal digital processing.

title: Quantum Machine Learning For Cyber-Physical Anomaly Detection In Unmanned Aerial Vehicles: A Leakage-Free Evaluation With Proxy-Audited Feature Sets
authors: Carlos A. Dur\'an Paredes, Javier E. Le\'on Calder\'on, Nicol\'as S\'anchez Perea, German Dar\'io D\'iaz, Camilo Segura Quintero
abstract: ArXiv:2605.19233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are cyber-physical systems whose attack surface spans networked avionics and on-board sensor fusion: a compromised GPS or battery module can mimic a benign mission segment and evade naive anomaly detectors. We present a leakage-free evaluation of quantum machine learning for UAV anomaly detection on the multi-sensor TLM:UAV benchmark. Three contributions support the study.
